title: CPAT Python
text:
CPAT Python


Coded CPAT overviewStatus, how a run works, testing, ways in · PowerPoint, latest version

CPAT Python (Coded CPAT) is the Python model of CPAT. It reproduces the Excel-AI prototypes number for number (every result code within 1e-9), runs one country and two scenarios in under a second, and is written to be read: one small function per equation, named with the codes of the Excel models. It runs from the command line, from Python or in a Shiny app.

1.1 Quick start
Everything you need to run Coded CPAT, find your way in its data and results, change it and test it.

title: 1  Using the model
text:
1.1.1 What Coded CPAT is

A replication. Coded CPAT computes what the Excel-AI prototypes compute: the mitigation model (prices, power, fuel use, emissions, revenues, GDP effects, welfare, for 2022-2041) and the household distribution module (incidence by decile). The tests check every output code against Excel-AI’s values.
Readable code. Each equation of the equation list is one small function or one marked line, with the code names of the Excel models (ener energy use, atp after-tax price, co2 emissions, …).
One entry point. cpat_model.run(scenarios, settings) serves the command line, the Shiny app and the tests.
Bugs are not copied. Where Excel-AI has a bug, Coded CPAT fixes it and registers it (Appendix B); everything else follows Excel-AI exactly.



1.1.2 Install
Python 3.12 (3.13 works), from the coded/ folder of the repository:
conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate cpat_p
# or, without conda:
pip install -r requirements.txt -r dev-requirements.txt


1.1.3 Run it
Command line: a scenario-set file in, results out.
python run_model.py                                      # Excel-AI's six scenarios for Egypt
python run_model.py my_set.csv --scenarios 1 2 --xlsx    # your own scenario set; also one workbook
Results go to coded/outputs/ (or --out): mitigation_EGY.csv (one row per output code, years 2022-2041) and distribution_EGY.csv (basket and ten deciles).
From Python:
import cpat_model
from cpat_model.inputs import read_scenario_set

results = cpat_model.run(read_scenario_set())                   # dummy database, Egypt
results.by_code('EGY').loc['egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2']             # CO2 of scenario 2, by year
results.distribution_by_code('EGY').loc['egy.distn.net.tot.dec.ove.2']   # net effect by decile
The app: shiny run app.py (from coded/), then open the address it prints. Build carbon-tax scenarios, run them, and look at tables and graphs.


1.1.4 Speed
A first run in a session takes about 3 seconds (reading the data and the baseline). After that, a run of one country and two scenarios takes under a second: the baseline, the data steps and every scenario already run are cached, so only changed scenarios are computed.


1.1.5 Where things are







Path
What

title: 1  Using the model
text:
1.2 The database

1.2.1 In short

Format: tidy CSV. One table per file; long format, one observation per row; standard keys first, then value (or one column per variable). Country codes are ISO3 in upper case (EGY).
Where: data/Public01/tidy/ in this repository: the dummy database. It is data edition Public01 (data/editions.csv): the public data, and Egypt’s rows of the six proprietary tables perturbed within ±3% (identities kept); every country can be added. The full database (every country, the proprietary tables) lives in a private repository, never in this one.
Choosing a database: Settings(database='dummy') (default) reads data/Public01/tidy/; Settings(database='full') reads the folder named by the environment variable FULL_DATA_PATH (set it in coded/.env or your shell). Command line: --database full.
One table list: data/Public01/tidy/_manifest.csv lists every table (218 tables, plus the layout entries of the 13 tabs kept at their cell addresses), its kind, its legacy source, its keys, rows and whether it is proprietary. Appendix A shows them all with their columns.
Tidy is the source of truth. The legacy-compatible workbook data/Public01/legacy_xlsx/CPAT_LegacyData.xlsx is written from it by data/scripts/tidy_convert.py (tested round trip), for pasting into legacy CPAT and for Excel-AI.
Master table: data/catalog.csv lists every data table: tidy file, Excel tab, proprietary or not, provenance, and the legacy data sources.







WarningProprietary data



Six tables are proprietary: energy balances (energy_balances), energy consumption (energy_consumption), domestic prices (prices_domestic), the GTAP input-output tables (io_gtap), the household survey (hh_survey) and the transport scatter data (tran_scatter). Their full versions, and anything computed from them, are never committed to this repository. The repository holds them only perturbed (Egypt’s rows within ±3%, identities kept; data/README.md).




1.2.2 What a table looks like
data/Public01/tidy/energy_balances.csv            data/Public01/tidy/prices_domestic.csv
country,year,unit,flow,fuel,value        country,year,code,value
EGY,2022,ktoe,cement,ecy,1158.39         EGY,2019,VAT_WEO,0.14
EGY,2022,ktoe,cement,coa,1422.24         EGY,2019,mit.sp.coa.pow,3.88
Keys come first (country, year, codes), then the value. Years, fuels, sectors and price codes are columns of keys, not column headers. A blank is a missing value.

1.2.4 Adding or updating data

Edit the tidy table (add the country’s rows with the same keys), then rewrite the legacy workbook (python data/scripts/tidy_convert.py to-xlsx, see data/README.md).
Run the data tests: python -m pytest data/tests (the round trip tidy to workbook to tidy must give every value back, and the committed workbook must be current).
Run the model for the country (python run_model.py --countries XXX). A country needs at least its energy balance and domestic prices; the app offers only countries that have both.

Every data table, with its proprietary status and provenance: data/catalog.csv (data/README.md).

title: 1  Using the model
text:
1.3 Scenarios and inputs

1.3.1 In short

A scenario set is one CSV file: one row per input, one column per scenario. Scenario 1, the baseline, comes first; every other scenario is compared with it.
Inputs are named as in Excel-AI (NameOfParameter, the Scenarios tab; ScenarioDefinition to 1.1.0): CPLevelTarget, CPIntro, IntEnerPricForeSource, … Every input is listed in Appendix A.
The example is Excel-AI’s own set, data/inputs/scenarios_excel_ai.csv (six scenarios for Egypt). Copy it and change the values to make your own.



1.3.2 The file
row,name,label,unit,1,2,3
,_ScenarioName,Scenario name,,Baseline (no carbon price),Carbon price 20/tCO2 from 2027,...
,_Countries,Countries,ISO3,EGY,EGY,EGY
...,CPIntro,Year the carbon price starts,year,2027,2027,...
...,CPLevelTarget,Carbon price in the target year,USD/tCO2,0,20,...







Column
Meaning




row
The input’s row in Excel-AI’s Scenarios tab (blank for meta rows and Python additions)


name
The input’s name (NameOfParameter); rows starting with _ are meta rows (scenario name, countries)


label, unit
What it is and its unit, for people


1, 2, …
The value in each scenario



Values are as in Excel-AI: numbers, or the options of Excel-AI’s drop-down lists as text (Yes*, Linear*, IMF). A star marks Excel-AI’s default option.


1.3.3 Rules

Scenario 1 is the baseline and must be the first column. It is run first; the policy scenarios read their baseline values from it.
Global inputs come from scenario 1 (D16): a few inputs hold for the whole run (results year, last historical price year, social cost of carbon settings, price controls, …; GLOBAL_INPUTS in cpat_model/inputs/scenarios.py). If another scenario sets a different value, the run warns and uses the baseline’s, as Excel-AI does.
Countries come from --countries on the command line, else from the _Countries row, else Egypt. All scenarios of a run use the same countries.
An unknown input name is an error (inputs['X'] raises), so a typo cannot pass silently.



1.3.4 Making a scenario
To add a carbon tax of 50 USD/tCO2 by 2035 starting in 2027: copy the column of scenario 2, give it a new number and name, and set CPIntro = 2027, CPOutro = 2035, CPLevelTarget = 50. The app does the same from its form: its scenarios are copies of Excel-AI’s carbon-tax column with the form’s values written over them (The app).

title: 1  Using the model
text:
1.4 Results

1.4.1 In short

Every result has an output code, the same as Excel-AI’s: <country>.mit.<variable>.<sector>.<fuel>.<scenario> for mitigation (e.g. egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2: total CO2 of scenario 2; the variable is one code token as in Excel-AI 1.4.0: egy.mit.gdp_pos_usd.all.all.2 for variable gdp.pos.usd) and <country>.distn.<variable>....<group> for distribution.
results.by_code(country): a table of every mitigation row, index = output code, columns = years 2022-2041.
results.distribution_by_code(country): every row of the Distribution sheet, columns 0 (the basket, all households) and 1-10 (the deciles, poorest first).
run_model.py writes both as CSV, the mitigation table with each row’s variable, sector, fuel, description and unit.



1.4.2 Reading a code

Meaning

Subsector, sector group, or the total


Fuel
gso, nga, ecy, tot
Fuel, or all fuels


Scenario
1, 2
The scenario’s column number



Some rows have no sector or fuel (egy.mit.cptraj.2, the carbon price path). A few Excel-AI rows have a different code from their variable (totals use tot, revenue rows rev.usd): core/variables.csv gives the code of every row.

1.4.4 In Python
r = cpat_model.run(read_scenario_set())
t = r.by_code('EGY')
t.loc['egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2'] / t.loc['egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.1'] - 1     # CO2 change against the baseline
r.states[2]['co2']                                                       # the same row as a labelled array

title: 1  Using the model
text:
1.5 Editing the model

1.5.1 The rules in ten lines
The full rules are the Python norms (Appendix B); these are the ones you need first.

Excel-AI is the specification. Python computes what Excel-AI computes, row for row, except Excel-AI’s bugs.
Bugs are not copied; issues are. A bug (Excel-AI does not compute what it means to) is fixed in Python and registered the same day; an issue (a potential improvement) is logged and copied as it is (Appendix B).
Codes are shared. Inputs, variables and outputs carry Excel-AI’s names; never invent a second name.
One equation, one function. Each equation of the equation list is a small function or one marked line, citing its id (EQ-M3.1).
The order is written once, in cpat_model/mitigation/chain.py.
Data only through cpat_model/data/, inputs only through cpat_model/inputs/.
Every change is tested against Excel-AI’s values (Testing) before it is committed.
Never commit proprietary data or anything computed from them.
Log every finished task in CAVEATS.md (what, outputs, checks, caveats) and tick coded/TODO.md.
Readability first: short functions, Excel-AI’s names, a comment wherever Python departs from the obvious.



1.5.2 The code map



Folder
What




cpat_model/__init__.py
run(): the entry point; the version


cpat_model/settings.py
Run settings: database, countries, years


cpat_model/core/
The run loop (loop.py), rows of a block (rows.py), index sets, the variable registry (variables.csv), Excel-AI constants and tables


cpat_model/data/
Reads the tidy tables


cpat_model/inputs/
Reads scenario sets


cpat_model/mitigation/
The blocks of Excel-AI’s Mitigation sheet (The mitigation blocks); *_data.py are the data steps


cpat_model/distribution/
The distribution module (The distribution module)


cpat_model/results/
Results


cpat_model/air_pollution/, transport_cobenefits/
Placeholder modules (Excel-AI’s typed values)





1.5.3 How a block looks
def step(state, db, inputs, settings, baseline, t):
    """EQ-M3.2: fuel use, emissions and revenues of every fuel block in year t."""
    R = year_rows(state, settings)                   # the rows of the year loop
    k = settings.years.index(t)
    at = lambda var, sector=None, fuel=None: R.at(var, k, sector, fuel)
    ...
    ener = R.set('ener', k, use + leak, s, f)        # row ener.<s>.<f>, year t
    R.set('co2', k, ener * pj * co2ef, s, f)         # row co2.<s>.<f>
A row is set with R.set(variable, year index, values, sector, fuel) and read with R.at(...); values are arrays by country. The baseline’s value of a row (Excel-AI’s REFCOL) is reference(R, baseline, k, var, sector, fuel).


1.5.4 Changing an equation

Find the Excel-AI rows (the formulas: excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Formulas.md; the variable’s rows: core/variables.csv).
Change the function; keep the equation id.
Update the equation in cpat_documentation/equations/equations.yaml and run python make_equations.py.
Run the tests. If Excel-AI changed too, re-extract the reference values first (Testing).



1.5.5 Adding a block
Write the block in its module (sheet order, equation ids), add it to chain.py, add its variables to BUILT in cpat_testing/test_mitigation.py, add the equations, run the tests, log the task. Architecture explains the stages a block can run in.

title: 1  Using the model

1.6 Testing

1.6.1 In short

Run pytest from coded/ before every commit (about one minute). Everything must pass.
The main test is the comparison with Excel-AI: every output code of every built block, for Egypt’s scenarios 1 and 2, every year 2022-2041, must equal Excel-AI’s stored value within 1e-9 (relative where the value is above 1). The distribution sheet is compared the same way, basket and deciles.
Known differences are the codes where Coded CPAT fixes an Excel-AI bug that is still open in the prototype; the tests leave them out of the match and check that they do differ (Appendix B).

1.6.5 The comparison with Excel-AI
The reference values are Excel-AI’s values, extracted from the release of EXCEL_AI_VERSION (found by version, excel_ai/core/tools/release.py) into CSV files. Releases from 1.2.0 store values to 2035 only: the later years, and the engineer scenario, come from the release activated as the Master does (formulas copied to 2041) and recalculated in LibreOffice, which first checks that it equals the stored values:
python cpat_testing/compare/extract_excel_ai.py                  # inputs, variables, tables (and the reference to 1.1.0)
python cpat_testing/compare/make_recalc_reference.py             # reference/excel_ai_<version>.csv, all years, and _engineer.csv
python cpat_testing/compare/extract_excel_ai.py --distribution   # reference/excel_ai_distribution_<version>.csv
The files keep the codes as the release writes them; compare.reference() reads them in the form Coded CPAT writes (Excel-AI 1.4.0, cpat_model/core/codes.py), so a reference of an older release compares too (the stored-outputs test reads the 1.1.0 StoredOutputs that way).
cpat_testing/compare/compare.py compares a results table with them code by code and year by year and reports the first year that differs. For a quick look while working:
from cpat_testing.compare.compare import compare, reference, summary
report = compare(results.by_code('EGY'), ref=reference())
summary(report[report.first_bad.notna()])


1.6.6 Known differences
cpat_testing/compare/known_differences.py lists, by Excel-AI bug, the codes where Python differs on purpose. When Excel-AI ships the fix of a bug, delete its entry: the codes must then match again. A test fails if a listed code matches Excel-AI (the entry is out of date) or if an unlisted code differs.

Only Egypt has its base tables in the dummy database; other countries need the full database (a run stops with a clear message)

title: 2  How it works
text:
2.1 Architecture
The structure of the code: how a run goes, the mitigation blocks, the distribution module, the app and the versions.

title: 2  How it works
text:
2.1.1 A run
cpat_model.run(scenarios, settings) (core/loop.py):

Settings. The database, countries and years (2022-2041), and the global inputs taken from scenario 1.
Scenario 1 (the baseline) first, then each policy scenario (D15). Each scenario runs in three stages over the blocks of mitigation/chain.py:









Stage
When
Blocks




Prepare
Once, all years at once: nothing here depends on a model quantity
Module values, header (macro series), policies, prices before new policies, power costs, fuel prices by subsector, Pigouvian taxes, road data


Year loop
For t = 2022 … 2041, every year block in order
GDP level, power, fuel use, totals, price averages, CO2, other GHGs, local pollutants, revenues, carbon-pricing indicators, module inputs, GDP effects, external balance, road engineer model, transport externalities, welfare


Finish
Once, after the year loop
NDC rows (they read the baseline at the target year)




Distribution. Each scenario against scenario 1 in the analysis year.
Results. The states of all scenarios, read by Results.

The only link from one year to the next, apart from a block’s own lagged rows, is the GDP effect: revenue of year t moves GDP from t+1.


2.1.2 Rows and the state

A row is one Excel-AI row: variable, sector, fuel; values by country and year.
Rows (core/rows.py) holds a block’s rows as numpy arrays while it computes them: put (all years), set (one year), at, of; finish stores them in the state. All year blocks share one Rows (gdp.year_rows).
State is one scenario’s rows. Block rows stay numpy arrays; state[var] builds a labelled xarray array (dimensions sector, fuel, country, year) only when something outside the blocks reads it. Entries starting with _ are working data, not results.
Data steps (*_data.py) compute what Excel-AI computes on its Inputs sheet, per country, from the tidy tables.



2.1.3 Caching and speed








Cache
Key
Effect




Baseline run
Scenario-1 inputs, database folder, settings
A run with the same baseline does not recompute it


Data steps (rows.cached)
The same, plus the step
Shared by every scenario of that baseline


Scenario runs
Baseline, scenario number, inputs
A rerun computes only the scenarios that changed


Database tables
The folder
Each table read once per session



One country and two scenarios run in under a second once the baseline is cached; six unchanged scenarios rerun in about 0.15 s. The caches live for the Python session: a changed data file needs a new session. Do not modify the arrays of a cached state.

title: 2  How it works

2.2 The mitigation blocks
Each block replicates one part of Excel-AI’s Mitigation sheet. The order of the run is mitigation/chain.py; the method of each block, with its equations and pseudocode, is explained in the CPAT-AI Model tab (shared with Excel-AI) and every equation is in its equation list; the test of each block is a BUILT entry of cpat_testing/test_mitigation.py.

title: 2  How it works
text:
2.3 The distribution module
cpat_model/distribution/ replicates Excel-AI’s Distribution prototype (version 0.1.3): the effect of each scenario on households by decile, in the analysis year (input YearDistn), against scenario 1.








Module
Replicates
What




mapping.py
Sheet DistMapping, the data tabs
Survey and elasticities, the input-output data of the country (fuel-group use, category coefficients), programmes, pass-through, ASPIRE, Gini weights


incidence.py
Sheet Distribution, sections 1-11
Settings; price changes from mitigation; indirect price changes through the input-output table; price factors, budget shares, direct and indirect effects; survey to national accounts; revenue recycling (income-tax cut, public investment, current spending, targeted transfers); net effect and Gini; chart rows; price changes by production sector



Every row has 11 columns: 0 the basket (all households) and 1-10 the deciles. incidence.run returns the rows by output code; the run stores them in Results.distribution. The equations are D1.1-D1.6 and B1.1-B1.8 (the equation list).

title: 2  How it works
text:
2.4 The app
shiny run app.py from coded/. The app (cpat_shiny/) builds carbon-tax scenarios, runs them through cpat_model.run and shows the results.







Section
What it does




Manual inputs
A scenario: name, countries (only those with data), carbon tax start and target year and level, after the target year, international price source, fuels and sectors covered


Scenarios
The scenarios built so far; load or save them as CSV; run them


Raw results
Rows of chosen variables (energy use, CO2, retail prices, taxes, subsidies, supply price) by country, sector, fuel and scenario; download as a workbook


Indicators
Carbon price, CO2, energy use, revenue, real GDP, against the baseline; download


Visualizations
Energy use by sector and by fuel, change by fuel, domestic prices, emissions by sector, net effect on households by decile


Documentation
The method notes



How the app’s inputs reach the model (cpat_shiny/server_logic/run_model.py): scenario 1 is Excel-AI’s baseline column; each app scenario is a copy of Excel-AI’s carbon-tax column with the form’s values written over it.







App input
Model input




Carbon tax start, target year
CPIntro, CPOutro


Carbon tax start, target level
CPLevelStart, CPLevelTarget


After the target year
ExtendCarbonPriceBeyondOutro


International price source
IntEnerPricForeSource (baseline too)


Fuels, sectors covered
MCov<Fuel>, MCov<Sector> (none selected: Excel-AI’s coverage)



The scenarios of one run share their baseline, so they must share countries and price source. The app has no controls yet for fuel subsidies, ETS or feebates.

title: 2  How it works
text:
2.5 Versions and releases

Version number (D14): <Excel-AI version>p<Python version>. 1.0.0p1.0, the first full release, is Python version 1.0 of the replication of Excel-AI 1.0.0 (and Distribution 0.2.0, then numbered 1.0.0). The current version, 1.3.1p1.5 (2026-11-01), is Python version 1.5 of the replication of Excel-AI 1.3.1 (and Distribution 0.5.1; Distribution has its own 0.x line since 1.3.1): it reads data edition Public01 (the six proprietary tables perturbed), with the reference values extracted from Excel-AI 1.3.1, runs the engineer road model switched on (TrModel = Engineer) as Excel-AI does, and writes the output codes of Excel-AI 1.4.0 (CODES_VERSION, cpat_model/core/codes.py). cpat_model.__version__ holds it; EXCEL_AI_VERSION and DISTRIBUTION_VERSION (cpat_model/__init__.py) name the workbooks the reference values come from.
Changelog: coded/CHANGELOG.md, one row per release (version, date, what changed, the largest difference against Excel-AI).
A release: all tests pass; the comparison with the Excel-AI version named in the number is complete (known differences listed); CHANGELOG.md row; CAVEATS.md entry; this book and the Word copies regenerated; git tag coded-v<version>.
When Excel-AI releases: re-extract the reference values, align Python with the prototype’s bug fixes (delete their known differences), run the tests, and release <new Excel-AI version>p1.0 (the Python part counts Python-only changes within one Excel-AI version).

B.2.1 1. The request (user, 2026-10-29), cleaned up

1.1 Goal
Build the full Python model (“Coded CPAT”) that directly replicates the mitigation and distribution modules of Excel-AI (excel_ai/CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm, CPAT-AI-Distribution-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm). The numbers must match Excel-AI. The overall norm is: always follow Excel-AI. Where an Excel-AI choice looks strange or wrong, report it to the user rather than silently departing; known departures from legacy CPAT are already tracked in the register (bugs L, issues I, departures LD, upgrades U).
The purpose of the code is full human readability: a reader with the methodology in one hand should be able to find each equation in the code in the other.


1.2 Ways the model is run

From saved scenarios: a table of scenario inputs in the MTInputs form (one row per NameOfParameter, one column per scenario), as legacy CPAT and Excel-AI ScenarioDefinition.
From a reactive Shiny user interface (later), which populates the same inputs dynamically.
Both use an advanced inputs file as well: time series and longer-form inputs of different types (the legacy Manual inputs tab).

The code runs many countries and many scenarios in one call (batch, comparisons), and one country with two or more scenarios (the main user interface).


1.3 Data: databases
Python and Excel-AI both run from the same databases. A database holds two or more complete sets of data:








Set
Contents
Where




Full
Every table, including the six proprietary tables
A separate, private repository (never this one)


Public
Every table except the six proprietary tables: energy balances (Balances), energy consumption (EnergyCons), domestic prices (Prices_dom), the GTAP input-output table (IO_GTAP), the household survey (HHSurvey) and the transport scatter data (Tran_Scatter)
This repository (data/)



This mirrors how Excel-AI and legacy CPAT work (legacy NoPropData workbooks lack the same four tables).


1.4 Testing

Compare Python with Excel-AI systematically.
Compare Python or Excel-AI with legacy CPAT.
In each case first for one country, then for all.
For these comparisons use a systematic dataset: the public set (full except the six proprietary tables), with the six tables filled the same way in every model.



1.5 Documentation and readability

The methodology is in docs/01_MainDocumentation/*.qmd. A website will be built from qmd (to HTML), with tabs for Excel-AI and for Python.
Plan the Python project in a human-readable way too, in qmd (markdown with extras) that can be built into the website and into Word.
An equation list: an executive summary with the core equations of each part, and appendices with all the adjustments. It uses the Greek letters and index letters of the methodology documentation; indices are shown only where they add clarity (otherwise the text says which indices an equation ranges over).
A parallel version with code names instead of Greek letters, using the authoritative list of CPAT variable codes (e.g. ener), the codes map in excel_ai/.
Box diagrams of the modular structure.
A separate NORMS and TODO for the Python project. Most Excel norms (formatting) do not apply; the overriding norm is to follow Excel-AI.



1.6 Structure

Decide up front whether the model computes everything for year t (all modules, including air pollution and transport co-benefits) before moving to year t+1.
Placeholder modules for air pollution and transport co-benefits, with their imports and exports defined now. Transport co-benefits will later be related to the transport (engineer) mitigation model.
Switchable core equations. The structure must allow later switching between forms of the core equations through one global switch: simple-CPAT (basic CPAT equations for every sector, power included), standard-CPAT (engineering power and transport models on), CPAT partial adjustment, CES partial adjustment (taking the CES-compatible price of the energy service), and CDPM (SISEPUEDE) plus FTT-like. Excel-AI implements its core equations as LAMBDA formulas; the Python forms play the same role. Only the Excel-AI form is built now.
Keep the existing, clean folder structure of coded/ as the starting point; do not clutter the core folders with working files; prefer a subfolder (with one pointer file at the top) over more than three new files in a folder. Recommend improvements to the structure, then make them.



1.7 Sequence of work

Plan the folder and code structure for readability (this document, NORMS.md, the diagrams).
The equation list (Greek letters) and its parallel version with code names.
Design choices: documented here (section 10) and gone through with the user, question by question.
The detailed plan (section 11 and coded/TODO.md), then the build.




B.2.2 2. Principles

Follow Excel-AI. The numbers of Coded CPAT equal Excel-AI’s, code by code, year by year; a difference is a defect of one of the two, found and registered. Through Excel-AI, Coded CPAT inherits the replication rule (never replicate a legacy bug; replicate and track every legacy issue).
Readable first. One equation, one function, with the equation in the docstring as in the equation list; names from the codes map; no hidden constants; the model order written once (mitigation/chain.py). Speed comes second, and is reached by working on whole arrays of countries and scenarios at once, not by obscure code.
One model, many front ends. One entry point, cpat_model.run(scenarios, database, settings), used by the command line (scenario files, many countries and scenarios), the Shiny app (one country, two or more scenarios, reactive) and the tests.
Same inputs, same data, same codes as Excel-AI. Scenario inputs are MTInputs rows by NameOfParameter; advanced inputs are the legacy Manual inputs, Settings and Constants; data come from the same databases; results carry the Excel-AI output codes.
Structure that allows change. The core demand equations sit behind slots that the scenario input ModelForm can fill with other forms (D4); downstream modules (distribution, air pollution, transport co-benefits) talk to mitigation through declared interfaces.
Documents from one source. qmd for people, generated Word copies, md for guides; the equation list in one source file for both of its versions.



B.2.3 3. Folder structure

3.1 Principles

Keep what is clean. The top level of coded/ stays as it is: cpat_model/ (the model), cpat_shiny/ (the app), cpat_testing/ (tests), cpat_documentation/ (documents), and the entry points and configuration files. Only NORMS.md is added at the top.
The package reads like the model. Inside cpat_model/, one subpackage per block of Excel-AI, named for what it computes, and one file, mitigation/chain.py, that lists the blocks in the order they run. A reader learns the model by reading chain.py, then each block in turn.
Shared machinery in one place (core/), the switchable equation forms in another (forms/), so model blocks hold only equations.
Inputs and data at the edge. Only inputs/ reads scenario files and only data/ reads databases; model code receives arrays.
Documents in cpat_documentation/, one subfolder per kind (project, equations, developer, user), with qmd sources and generated Word copies.
No working files in the core folders (NORMS 2.2): kept comparison scripts in cpat_testing/compare/, run outputs in coded/outputs/ (git-ignored).

4.2 Two passes, three stages (D1, D15: recommended options)
Excel-AI computes year by year with no circular reference: year t reads year t-1 and earlier (the GDP feedback reaches year t+1; power demand reads last year’s electricity price; capacity, vintages and vehicle stocks are recursions on t-1), and its only look-aheads read exogenous paths (the levelised variable cost of power over [t, 2041], built from prices and policies; next year’s manual capacity input). Policy scenarios also read scenario-1 values: stored ones (sheet BaselineCO2: CO2 by ETS sector, the calibration values in the GHG inventory year) and same-year ones (.ref, which reach the model only through the fiscal space and so GDP of t+1). Coded CPAT therefore runs the baseline first, then each policy scenario in turn (any number of scenarios; D15), each run in three stages:

B.2.7 7. Switchable equation forms
The behavioural core of CPAT is a small number of equations: fuel demand by sector and fuel, electricity demand, power supply (dispatch and investment) and road transport. Structure and computation
D1. Order of computation: year by year, or module by module? (decided: see the table)

A. Year by year, all modules within the year (recommended). Three stages: prepare (all years at once, for everything without feedback: policy paths, international prices, deflators, exogenous drivers, base-year calibration), the year loop (for t = base year + 1 … last year, every block of mitigation, then air pollution and transport co-benefits, for year t; GDP of year t feeds year t+1), finish (all-year results, welfare, indicators; distribution in its analysis year). This is how Excel-AI computes (years across, each year reads the year before; GDP feedback one year later, NORMS 5c), so the numbers match by construction, and later modules with feedback (Pigouvian taxes from air-pollution damages, endogenous transport) fit without restructuring.
B. Module by module, each over all years at once (vectorised in time). Simpler for blocks without feedback, but the GDP feedback and the lagged price terms force iterations over the whole model until convergence; harder to match Excel-AI exactly.
C. Hybrid by module: modules without feedback over all years, the rest year by year. Two styles in one code base; less readable.

D2. How quantities are held in the code (decided: see the table)

A. Labelled arrays, xarray (recommended). Each quantity is an array with named dimensions (country, scenario, year, fuel, sector, …). Equations read like the equation list (ener = ener_prev * (atp / atp_prev) ** eps_u), broadcasting by name; many countries and scenarios cost nothing extra. One added dependency.
B. pandas DataFrames with a MultiIndex (today’s coded/): familiar, but index alignment and year columns as strings make equations long.
C. numpy arrays with axis conventions: fastest, least readable.

D3. Variable names in the code (decided: see the table)

A. CPAT code stems (recommended): ener, atp, ctx, with _prev, _ref, _chg suffixes; a generated variable registry (from the codes map) gives description, unit, dimensions and Greek symbol. Matches Excel-AI and the outputs one to one; the codes are short but documented in every docstring.
B. Descriptive English names (fuel_use, after_tax_price) with the code as metadata: easier for a newcomer, but two vocabularies to keep aligned.

D4. The switch between equation forms (decided: see the table)

A. One global setting model_form, mapped to a form for each core-equation slot (recommended). Slots: fuel demand, electricity demand, power supply, road transport, service price (CES-compatible price). Forms: simple_cpat (elasticity equations for every sector, power and road included), standard_cpat (Excel-AI: engineering power and road models on; default), cpat_partial_adjustment, ces_partial_adjustment, cdpm_ftt (SISEPUEDE-like stock model plus FTT-like technology diffusion). Each form is a function with the same signature, registered in cpat_model/forms/, as Excel-AI’s LAMBDAs. Only standard_cpat (and the switches Excel-AI already has, e.g. TrModel) is built now.
B. As A, plus an override per slot or per sector (e.g. CES in buildings only). Can be added later without changing A.
Question: should the scenario inputs that already switch models in Excel-AI and legacy (road transport TrModel, power) stay per-scenario inputs, with model_form only setting their defaults? (recommended: yes)

D5. Input files (decided: see the table)

A. Scenario set: one table (xlsx or CSV), rows = the legacy MTInputs rows in order (NameOfParameter), columns = scenarios, plus a row per scenario for the country (or “all”); Excel-AI’s ScenarioDefinition pastes into it. Advanced inputs: one workbook with one tab per kind (time series by year, tables by fuel and sector, settings), defaults from Excel-AI Settings, Manual inputs and Constants. The Shiny app writes the same structures in memory.
B. YAML/JSON scenario files (one per scenario). Readable for programmers, but not the MTInputs form people use.
Question: can one scenario set mix countries (scenario x country pairs), or is a scenario always “these inputs for every listed country”? (recommended: inputs per scenario, applied to a list of countries; country-specific values through the advanced inputs)

D6. Databases (decided: see the table)

A. A database is a folder of CSV tables plus a manifest (datapackage.json: tables, columns, source, licence class, proprietary or not). public in this repository (data/), full in the private repository (same layout, the four proprietary tables added), dummy as today. The model reads DATA_ENVIRONMENT (public, full, dummy) and the path of the private repository from .env. Excel-AI’s data workbook is built from the same database (data_old/scripts/build_data_workbook.py), so both models read identical numbers.
B. A single database file (SQLite or DuckDB) per set. One file to move, fast queries; but binary, not diff-able in git.
Answered (user 2026-10-29): (i) the four proprietary tables are EnergyCons/Balances, Prices_dom, IO_GTAP and HHSurvey (2026-10-30: six, Balances and EnergyCons separately, plus Tran_Scatter); (ii) the systematic comparisons use the private full database where it is available, and the code must also allow dummy as an option; (iii) every table in data_old/dummy/ is dummy (not only the four), so a real public set (full minus the four tables) is not yet in this repository. Still open: where the public set lives and whether it is needed beyond full and dummy (see the design questions).

D7. The existing code in coded/ (decided: see the table)

A. Keep the folders, rebuild the model inside them block by block (recommended). cpat_shiny/, cpat_testing/, cpat_documentation/ and the data loaders stay; cpat_model/mitigation/ is rebuilt in Excel-AI block order on the new structure (D1-D4); each old subpackage is deleted when its replacement passes the Excel-AI comparison. Distribution (validated against Excel, 48 tests) is moved onto the new structure with its tests unchanged.
B. A new package next to the old one (e.g. cpat/), switch over at the end. Clean start, but two models in the repository for months.

Extract Excel-AI values by code (all codes, both scenario groups, every year) from the recalculated release workbook into a fixture table, one per release and country set, with a script in cpat_testing/compare/ (LibreOffice recalculation, as the Excel checks). D10. Placeholders for air pollution and transport co-benefits (decided: see the table)

A. Each module is a package with declared inputs (the codes it reads from mitigation: section 15 for air pollution, section 5 for transport co-benefits) and outputs (the codes it returns: air.vpm and concentration coefficients; tran.acc.km, tran.con.km, tran.rdm.km), and two hooks: prepare returns Excel-AI’s typed values (FromAirPollution, FromTransportCB), which feed the Pigouvian taxes before the year loop as in Excel-AI (I151); step(t) runs inside the year loop after the local pollutants and computes nothing until the module is built (section 4.5).

B.2.12 12. Excel-AI choices to flag
The overriding norm is to replicate Excel-AI. These choices are replicated as they are, but they are unusual enough that the user should know of them before the build; each is already in the register or proposed for it.

Stored scenario-1 values. Policy scenarios read baseline values stored on sheet BaselineCO2 and refreshed by the build (CO2 by ETS sector for the ETS cap and price estimate; the CO2 calibration factor and the energy-methane calibration in the GHG inventory year, 2024, which is after the base year). In Excel the results therefore depend on values stored by the last build, not on the current inputs. Coded CPAT computes them in its baseline pass (D15); the two agree only while Excel-AI’s stored values are current, which the comparison checks.
Scenario inputs that act as global settings. Some inputs are read from the scenario-1 column for every scenario (BiomassLeakage, BiomassNormal, the cooking-exemption inputs, cookstove efficiencies). In Coded CPAT they become run settings (D16), with a check that every scenario column agrees.
The road engineer model runs in every scenario whatever TrModel (issue I100); its outputs feed the transport co-benefit interface even when the elasticity form drives fuel use.
Module values typed for Egypt only. The air-pollution and transport co-benefit values (FromAirPollution, FromTransportCB) are typed from the legacy 465 run for Egypt; every other country reads 0 (I106), so Pigouvian taxes and those welfare terms are zero outside Egypt.
Pigouvian taxes by proxy (I151): marginal air-pollution damages use base-year fuel-use weights and typed values, so they do not respond to the scenario; this keeps the model acyclic (the tax enters the forward-looking power cost) and is the reason the placeholder modules feed the model in the prepare stage.
Fuel demand has no partial adjustment (MIm2): the full response to a price change happens in the year of the change. The cpat_partial_adjustment form addresses this later.
Investment need extrapolates required generation as Req(t)²/Req(t−1) instead of reading next year (L67 fix), and the levelised variable cost of power looks forward to 2041: both are exogenous, so they sit in the prepare stage.
ETS price by goal seek. The ETS permit price is found by an outer iteration over whole runs (run only on request); between runs it is a stored override row per scenario. Coded CPAT keeps the override as an advanced input and offers the iteration as a separate function.

Found while extracting the notation (full list: ../equations/reference/notation_from_methodology.md section 4). They do not change Coded CPAT, which follows Excel-AI, but the methodology should be corrected:

No in-model GDP equation: neither the multipliers chapter nor the mitigation chapter gives the GDP feedback; the equation list takes it from Excel-AI.
Undefined symbols: \(\epsilon_G\) in both power-demand equations (presumably \(\epsilon_Y\)); \(tex\) in Appendix C.
Markup sign: \(mu^T = gnc^{av} + tmc - hrp\) is then added to the price; to reproduce historical prices it must be \(hrp - gnc^{av} - tmc\).
Storage: the derivative of \(sst = 9v^2\) is written \(18v^2\) (should be \(18v\)); the long-term storage table does not match its formula.
Welfare: \(ddw\) uses \(nc\) for \(ncp\), and the text calls half the difference of the taxes their average.
Supply price: producer subsidies added in Appendix C, subtracted in the main text; base-year window 2019-2021 in one place, 2018-2022 in another.
Overloaded letters: \(g\) (sector group, generation, growth rate, consumption category, PIT gain), \(\gamma\) (six meanings), \(E\), \(p\)/\(P\), \(j\), \(i\); electricity coded ecy in mitigation and ely in distribution. The equation list fixes one meaning per letter within each part (its symbol appendix).

title: Appendix B — Project documents
text:
B.3 Python norms
Source: coded/NORMS.md.
Rules for every task in coded/. They add to the repository-wide ../excel_ai/core/NORMS.md, of which these sections apply to Python as written: 0 (never replicate a legacy bug; always replicate a legacy issue, and track it), 4 (inputs: MTInputs rows and NameOfParameter names), 6, 6b (task completion: CAVEATS.md; norms follow the lessons), 7 (methodology and version notes are different documents) and 8 (data). Its Excel sections (1-3, 5: columns, style, LAMBDA encoding, releases) do not apply, except where this file points to them.
The design choices behind these rules (D1-D16) were decided by the user on 2026-10-29: spec cpat_documentation/project/Spec.qmd section 10. A rule citing Dn follows that decision.







Section
Contents




0
The overriding norm: follow Excel-AI


1
Readability: equations, names, comments


2
Where things go (folders and files)


3
Model structure: dimensions, the year loop, modules, equation forms


4
Inputs: scenarios and advanced inputs


5
Data: databases


6
Results and codes


7
Tests and comparisons


8
Documents: qmd, Word, the website


9
Task completion and bookkeeping


10
Python conventions




B.3.1 The overriding norm: follow Excel-AI

Excel-AI is the specification. Coded CPAT replicates the mitigation and distribution modules of Excel-AI (../excel_ai/mitigation/releases/CPAT-AI-Mitigation_v<version>.xlsx, ../excel_ai/distribution/releases/CPAT-AI-Distribution_v<version>.xlsx, Distribution on its own 0.x line since 1.3.1; -Prototype_v<version>.xlsm to 1.1.0) number for number. When the methodology (../docs/01_MainDocumentation/), legacy CPAT and Excel-AI disagree, the code follows Excel-AI and the difference is already, or is then, in the register.
Which version (D14). The version of Coded CPAT is <Excel-AI version>p<Python version>, e.g. 1.0.0p1.0: Python version 1.0 of the replication of Excel-AI 1.0.0 (Excel-AI’s numbering was rebased on 2026-10-29: mitigation 9.0 is 0.9.0, distribution 1.3 is 0.1.3). The package states both (EXCEL_AI_VERSION, __version__), and each module docstring the Excel-AI version it replicates. Moving to a new Excel-AI version is a task of its own: port the changed rows (the Excel version log and ../excel_ai/core/CAVEATS.md list them), then rerun the comparison.
Bugs are not replicated; issues are (user rules 2026-10-29; root NORMS.md section 0 rule 6). Coded CPAT follows Excel-AI everywhere except in its bugs. A prototype bug (M: Excel-AI does not compute what it means to) is never replicated: register it the same day (OPEN_PROTO_BUGS in ../excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/register/issues_register.py), add its fix to the Excel-AI TODO list (../excel_ai/core/TODO.md), fix it here where the fix is obvious (a comment # bug M<n> fixed (Excel-AI: ...) at the line), list the codes that then differ from Excel-AI in cpat_testing/compare/known_differences.py (the tests check they differ), note it on TODO.md (section “Excel-AI bugs”) and tell the user. Where the fix is not obvious, keep Excel-AI’s formula (# Excel-AI bug M<n>, replicated until ...) and follow the prototype’s fixed version. An issue (a potential improvement) is logged for later and replicated for now. Never change Excel-AI’s behaviour silently.
Codes are shared. Variable codes, input names (NameOfParameter) and output codes are those of Excel-AI and the codes map ../excel_ai/core/CPAT-AI_CodesMap_v<version>.xlsx. Python never invents a second name for a quantity that has a code.
One register. Bugs and issues found while porting go in the one register (../excel_ai/bugs_and_legacy/register/issues_register.py; root NORMS.md section 0 rule 3), with module “Coded CPAT” where only Python is affected. Coded CPAT keeps no list of its own.



B.3.2 Readability: equations, names, comments
The purpose of the code is that a person with the equation list open can find, read and check every equation.

One equation, one function. Each equation of the equation list (cpat_documentation/equations/) is one small function (or one clearly marked line in a short function), named after the quantity it computes. Its docstring starts with the equation id and the equation in the notation of the equation list, then the Excel-AI rows it replicates:
def ener(ener_prev, atp, atp_prev, ...):
    """EQ-M4.1  Fuel use, CPAT constant-elasticity form.

    Q_t = Q_{t-1} * (1 + g_t)^(eps_Y) * (P_t / P_{t-1})^(eps_U) * ...      (over fuels i, sectors j)
    Excel-AI: Mitigation section 6, code ener.<sector>.<fuel>; Equations.md E69.
    """
Names are CPAT codes (D3). A variable that has a code in the codes map is called by its code stem in the code (ener, atp, ctx); the previous year adds _prev, the baseline (scenario 1) value adds _ref, a change against the baseline _chg (as Excel-AI .ref, .chg). The variable registry (cpat_model/core/variables.py, generated from the codes map) gives each code its description, unit, dimensions and Greek symbol. Names without a code (local helpers) are plain English words in snake_case, never single letters other than the index letters of the equation list.
The equation list and the code agree. An equation added, removed or changed in the code is changed in the equation list in the same task, and the other way round. A test lists every equation id and fails if one has no function or one function cites an unknown id.
No hard-coded numbers. Apart from 0, 1 and array positions, every number comes from the inputs, the data or a named constant in cpat_model/core/constants.py with its source and unit (as root NORMS.md section 3, “No hard-coded constants”).
Units in the registry, conversions in one place. Money units follow the Excel-AI vocabulary (USD m, LCU bn, USD/GJ, real or nominal; root NORMS.md section 3, “Money units”). A function body does not multiply by 1e3, 1e6 or 1e9; it calls a named conversion.
Short and flat. A function that needs scrolling is split. No clever one-liners, no metaprogramming in model code, no inheritance deeper than one level. Prefer explicit arguments to reading a global state.
Comments say why, not what. The docstring says what; a comment explains a choice, an Excel-AI quirk (with its register code, e.g. # I85: percentages typed as whole numbers, as legacy) or a unit.



B.3.3 Where things go (folders and files)

The layout is in README.md and in the spec, section 3. Code goes in cpat_model/ (the model), cpat_shiny/ (the app), cpat_testing/ (tests); documents in cpat_documentation/. The top of coded/ holds only the entry points (run_model.py, app.py), configuration (.env, environment files; the settings are cpat_model/settings.py) and the three guides (README.md, NORMS.md, TODO.md).
No working files in the core folders. Scratch scripts, notebooks, exports and one-off comparisons do not go in cpat_model/, cpat_shiny/ or cpat_testing/. Comparison scripts that are kept go in cpat_testing/compare/; run outputs go in coded/outputs/ (git-ignored); anything else temporary stays outside the repository.
Folders, not long lists. A folder gets at most three new files in one task; more become a subfolder with one pointer file (a README.md or __init__.py that says what is inside).
The package follows the model. cpat_model/mitigation/ has one subpackage per Excel-AI block, named for what it computes (policies, prices, power, fuel_use, revenues, emissions, gdp, …), and one file, chain.py, that lists the order in which the blocks run (spec section 3). A reader learns the model order from that one file.
No Old/, tmp_, new_, _v2 files. Git keeps the history; a replaced file is deleted in the task that replaces it.
Data never in coded/. All data are in ../data/ (root NORMS.md section 8); test fixtures with their tests (cpat_testing/**/data_expected/).



B.3.4 Model structure: dimensions, the year loop, modules, equation forms

Labelled arrays (D2). Model quantities are labelled arrays (xarray) with named dimensions: country, year, and the dimensions of the quantity (fuel, sector, tech, user, decile, …), using the index names of the equation list. Equations broadcast by name; no positional axis arithmetic in model code.
Baseline first, then scenario by scenario; three stages (D1, D15). A run takes any number of scenarios. The baseline (scenario 1) runs first, then each policy scenario in turn, reading the baseline values it needs (as Excel-AI’s BaselineCO2 and .ref). Each scenario run has three stages: prepare (everything that depends on no model quantity, for all years at once: policy paths, international prices and the price chain, power cost paths including the levelised variable cost, exogenous drivers, the module values that feed Pigouvian taxes), the year loop (for each year t, every block in the order of chain.py, each reading only year t and earlier years: all of mitigation, then the air-pollution and transport co-benefit modules for year t, then the GDP effect that reaches t+1), and finish (all-year results: carbon-pricing indicators, welfare, exports; then distribution in its analysis year). No equation reads a later model year (root NORMS.md 5c, circular references, rule 1); a look-ahead on exogenous paths belongs in prepare.
Countries together, scenarios in turn. Every function works for any number of countries at once (an array dimension); nothing loops over countries in model code. Scenarios run one after another (core/loop.py is the only scenario loop) and their results are joined along a scenario dimension. Scenario 1 is the baseline; _ref values are read from the baseline run in the same year, as Excel-AI’s ref_formula. Inputs that Excel-AI reads from the baseline column for every scenario are run settings, checked for agreement (D16).
Modules talk through declared interfaces. Each module declares what it reads and what it writes (codes). Downstream modules (distribution, air pollution, transport co-benefits) read only their declared inputs, as the Excel modules read only FromMitigation (root NORMS.md section 3, “Exports to modules”).
Switchable equation forms (D4). The demand equations (fuel demand, electricity demand, the CES service price) are called through the slots of cpat_model/forms/, never directly. The form is a scenario input, ModelForm, the last MTInputs row, set up the same way in Excel-AI and Python; the default, CPAT, is the Excel-AI form and the only one built until the user asks for another. ModelForm does not override the existing engineer-or-elasticity selectors of road transport and power (power always uses the engineer model). A new form never changes the numbers of CPAT, and is added to Excel-AI and Python in the same release.
Placeholder modules (D10). Air pollution and transport co-benefits each have prepare (Excel-AI’s typed module values, which feed the Pigouvian taxes) and step(t) (in the year loop after the local pollutants; empty until the module is built).



B.3.5 Inputs: scenarios and advanced inputs

Scenario inputs are MTInputs (D5). A scenario set is a table with the rows of legacy MTInputs (NameOfParameter, root NORMS.md section 4; the Excel-AI additions, ModelForm last, below them) and one column per scenario, each scenario run for a list of countries; the Shiny app builds the same table. Input keys are the NameOfParameter names, in legacy units (I85).
Advanced inputs (time series and longer-form inputs, the legacy Manual inputs tab and Excel-AI Settings) come from one advanced-inputs workbook per run (a tab per kind: time series, Manual inputs blocks, Settings, Constants; D5), with defaults from Excel-AI. Input files live in ../data/inputs/ (D6).
Validated once. Inputs are read and checked (names known, types, ranges, option values as legacy) in cpat_model/inputs/ before the model runs; model code never reads a raw input file.



B.3.6 Data: databases

Databases (D6; user 2026-10-29: tidy CSV). Coded CPAT reads tidy CSV (../data/Public01/tidy/: one table per file, long, standard keys, country ISO3 upper case), converted both ways from the legacy layout Excel-AI reads by ../data/scripts/tidy_convert.py (exact round trip, tested). A database is a folder of tidy tables with its _layout/, in the structure of ../data/ (input files under ../data/inputs/). Two exist: full (every table with its real values, including the six proprietary tables Balances, EnergyCons, Prices_dom, IO_GTAP, HHSurvey, Tran_Scatter; edition Full01, a private repository, never this one) and dummy (an edition of this repository, ../data/<edition>/tidy/, the default ../data/Public01/tidy/: the public tables, with the six proprietary tables perturbed within +-3%, identities kept; ../data/README.md). The code interface (each table the model reads) is the edition’s tidy manifest (../data/Public01/tidy/_manifest.csv), and a loader reads nothing it does not list. The choice is a setting (Settings.database; the edition: CPAT_DATA_EDITION, else the default of ../data/editions.csv; full: FULL_DATA_PATH, the tidy folder of the full database outside the repository). The systematic comparisons use full where it is available, with dummy as the option that always works (user 2026-10-29); every model in a comparison reads the same database.
Never commit proprietary data, nor results computed from them (root NORMS.md section 8).
Loaders read, never compute. cpat_model/data/ loads and reshapes tables to the model’s dimensions; any calculation on data is a model equation with an id.



B.3.7 Results and codes

Results are keyed by Excel-AI output codes (<variable>.<sector>.<fuel> as the prototype) and dimensions country, scenario, year, so every Python result can be set against the Excel-AI row with the same code. The codes take Excel-AI’s latest code form (1.4.0: every code variable one token, pav_leg; cpat_model/core/codes.py, CODES_VERSION); variables keep Excel-AI’s names (pav.leg). A comparison with an older release reads its codes through codes.current, never through a second name in the model. Excel-AI rows and tables are found by their code or heading, never by row number (sections and rows move between releases; check: the extractor finds every table by its heading).
Results belong to the scenario; differences as Excel-AI (root NORMS.md section 3c: x.ref, x.chg, x.pct only for strictly positive quantities; price changes are price indices; ratios from summed levels).



B.3.8 Tests and comparisons

Three levels. Unit tests per equation (small hand-checked cases); block tests against reference values by code for one country: first the existing Python recomputations of Excel-AI (../excel_ai/mitigation/checks/check_full.py, power_model_ref.py, transport_model_ref.py, distribution_ref.py; D8), then values extracted from the recalculated Excel-AI workbook (directly for the rows the recomputations lack); end-to-end comparisons (all codes, then all countries).
Tolerance. Python equals Excel-AI to a relative difference of 1e-9 (absolute 1e-9 near zero) unless a difference is explained and registered.
Comparison order: Python against Excel-AI, one country (Egypt), then all countries; Python or Excel-AI against legacy CPAT, one country, then all; always on the systematic dataset (section 5).
Speed (D11). One country with two scenarios runs in under 1 second for the user interface (data and the baseline run cached). Speed never costs readability: it comes from array operations and caching.
pytest passes before every commit. A failing comparison is not skipped or loosened to pass; it is fixed or registered.



B.3.9 Documents: qmd, Word, the website

qmd is the source. Documents for people (spec, plan, design choices, equation list, method notes) are Quarto markdown (.qmd) in cpat_documentation/; Word copies (.docx) are generated from them (cpat_documentation/make_docs.py), never edited by hand. Guides for agents and developers (README.md, NORMS.md, TODO.md) stay .md: GitHub shows them formatted, every tool reads them, and Quarto renders .md as well as .qmd, so they can join the website unchanged.
Diagrams are mermaid blocks in the qmd (Quarto draws them); make_docs.py renders them to PNG for Word.
Notation. The equation list uses the Greek letters and index letters of the methodology (../docs/01_MainDocumentation/); where the methodology has none, it says so and uses the Excel-AI note (../excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Equations.md). Its code version uses the codes map.
Methodology, not history (root NORMS.md section 7): the equation list and method notes describe the current model only.
The documentation book (user 2026-10-29; restructured 2026-10-31). The Coded CPAT documentation is a Quarto book, the website’s CPAT Python tab (#python), in the style of the methodology documentation: few chapters, each with many sections (user 2026-10-31). Chapter 1 Using the model (concise: quick start, the database first, scenarios, results, editing, testing), chapter 2 How it works, and two appendices: A data, inputs and variables (with the glossary), B project documents (bugs, spec, norms, plan). The method of each block and the equation list are in the CPAT-AI Model book (../docs/CPAT_model_documentation_qmd/, tab #model, user 2026-10-31), shared with Excel-AI: a change to the method of a block updates its chapter there the same day; the equation list is generated there from cpat_documentation/equations/equations.yaml. The chapters are written in ../docs/CPAT_coded_documentation_qmd/ (index.qmd, 01_Using_the_model.qmd, 02_How_it_works.qmd, _glossary.md; was cpat_documentation/guide/ until 2026-10-30); the appendices are generated from the code and data (../docs/CPAT_coded_documentation_qmd/make_qmd.py). New material goes into a section of these chapters, not a new chapter. The latest Coded CPAT deck is ../docs/presentations/03_Coded-CPAT_Overview_latest.pptx, written by cpat_documentation/presentation/build_deck.js and linked at the top of the tab. A task that changes how to run, edit or test the model, the database, the inputs or the results updates its chapter the same day; a task that changes the tests reruns make_qmd.py --tests (the test status) before quarto render.



B.3.10 Task completion and bookkeeping
As root NORMS.md section 6: every finished task gets a ../excel_ai/core/CAVEATS.md entry; open work is in TODO.md (tick it, add the follow-ups); a lesson with a cause that can repeat becomes a norm here, with its check (root section 6b).


B.3.11 Python conventions

Python 3.12, pandas, numpy, xarray (environment.yml, requirements.txt); new dependencies only with a reason in the task’s CAVEATS.md entry.
Type hints on public functions; ruff for lint and format.
Functions are pure: inputs in, results out, no file or global state inside model code. Reading files happens in cpat_model/data/ and cpat_model/inputs/ only.
The one public entry point is cpat_model.run(...) (spec section 3); run_model.py, the Shiny app and the tests all call it.

B.4 The plan and open work
Source: coded/TODO.md.
Status key: ☐ not started · ◐ in progress · ☑ done · ☒ closed without doing (superseded) (ticked items leave at the next update; their record is ../excel_ai/core/CAVEATS.md). Excel work: ../excel_ai/core/TODO.md. Rules: NORMS.md.
The project (user 2026-10-29): the full build of Coded CPAT, a human-readable Python model that replicates the mitigation and distribution modules of Excel-AI number for number. Specification, design choices and the plan in words: cpat_documentation/project/Spec.qmd (Word copy Spec.docx). The phases below are the plan’s checklist; section numbers refer to the spec.

B.4.1 Shiny app on Excel-AI’s User-defined page (user 2026-11-15: “a new shiny interface, based on the Excel”)
Done: cpat_shiny/ rebuilt (shiny run app.py; screenshots cpat_documentation/app_screenshot.png, app_dashboard.png). Tabs: User-defined scenario (Excel-AI 1.9.56’s tab: sections Scenario, A-F and the global policies; 531 controls generated from ../excel_ai/mitigation/policy_ui/ui_spec.py through cpat_shiny/user_defined/page.json, written by python -m cpat_shiny.user_defined.build_page; defaults = the tab’s values in the latest workbook), Scenarios and run (countries, price source; the scenario set: add, edit, remove, upload and download CSV in the Pre-defined layout; run), Data (upload tidy tables or an edition zip, server-side temporary folder), Dashboard (key results by scenario: carbon price, CO2, revenue, GDP, prices, distribution, transport co-benefits), Results (graphs, raw results XLSX, indicators XLSX, documentation). The adapter server_logic/run_model.py builds each column as Excel-AI’s Pre-defined (the page’s inputs, the derived .m rows by Excel-AI’s formulas, the template for the rest): the default scenario equals Excel-AI’s scenario 2 on every row (test_default_user_scenario_is_excel_ai_scenario_2; also equal to column 2 of ../data/inputs/scenarios_excel_ai.csv).

Information cells (grey) of the page are blank: Excel fills them from the data (existing subsidies and taxes, VAT gaps, price controls now) or the model (ETS cap and permit price); fill them from the run’s results (not from the data tables, which stay on the server) after a run.
Excel’s information charts of the page (carbon price path, coverage, energy price components, fiscal multipliers, EV share) are not drawn; the Dashboard tab has the results.
The settings of tab Settings other than the price source and the global policies (e.g. TrModel, TcbMode, TCB_) keep the scenario set’s values; expose more if users need them.
Uploaded user data: the stored baseline table (inputs/baseline_co2.csv) stays the edition’s when only tables are uploaded (an edition zip brings its own); the model’s ETS baseline reads it.
Publishing (shinyapps.io): the bundle needs coded/ and data/Default (the model reads the edition from the repository); it must not include excel_ai/ (page.json makes the app independent of it). The run cache of cpat_model.core.loop is per process (shared by sessions).
